abstract: Purpose: Reliable functional mapping of the language network and preoperative assessment of language lateralization are essential for safe and effective craniotomy in patients with lesions in language-eloquent brain regions, yet existing fMRI language paradigms are often time-consuming and place substantial cognitive and economic demands on patients and diagnostic services. Methods: We therefore tested ecologically valid German stimulus sets designed to optimize measurement efficiency. Forty-three healthy participants (mean age = 38 years, range = 20 - 64; 24 women) were scanned on a 3T MRI while reading or listening to 4-, 8-, and 12-word sentences and pseudoword lists or texts, each followed by a decision task. Sentences were selected from German literary classics and text passages from general-interest science magazines and matched across conditions for lexical and structural properties. Results: Region-of-interest analyses in subject-specific, functionally defined language-sensitive regions showed robust activation of the left-hemispheric language network across modalities. Within participants, texts elicited significantly larger effect sizes than sentences, and longer sentences generally produced stronger responses than shorter ones. Task manipulations expected to increase cognitive demand (short 4-word sentences with frequent probes, coherent texts requiring deeper semantic integration) did not enhance responses in the domain-general multiple demand network, indicating that executive-control activity did not overshadow language-selective activation, whereas substantial overlap between default mode and language-sensitive regions in the left temporal lobe was consistent with relatively automatic processing of connected language. Conclusions: These findings indicate that ecologically valid sentence- and text-based paradigms can provide efficient, language-specific fMRI protocols for preoperative diagnostics and individualized presurgical planning in patients with lesions near language-eloquent cortex.
